children: Albertsons earnings call started Tuesday with a mea culpa and followed with a for sale sign.
"Our performance has fallen short," said Executive Chair Meg Whitman. "Everything should be on the table as we figure out how Albertsons should be structured to better compete in the years ahead."
Whitman, the former CEO of eBay and Hewlett Packard, came to Albertson's one month ago to help the management team with strategy. She said the grocer "must turn things around."

The Idaho-based grocer is exhibit A for problems in the supermarket business. With food prices rising, shoppers are cutting back on trips and spending. Costs for everything from energy to labor are surging. The company's stock is down about 26% so far this year, and is on pace for its worst year since 2022.

Albertsons is still digging out of its 2022 attempt to sell itself to Kroger for $20 billion. Executives at the grocery chain have said two years of focusing on the deal with its rival put it behind on key business decisions, such as closing or investing in underperforming stores. It has brands including Safeway, Jewel-Osco and ACME across about 2,200 stores, primarily concentrated in the western half of the country, the Northeast and Chicago.

Albertsons' struggles after the deal collapsed were predicted by its former CEO, Vivek Sankaran, in a Portland, Ore., federal courtroom in 2024. He said the supermarket chain would close stores or lay off workers if a judge rejected Kroger's takeover because of rising competition and mounting economic pressures.
The "grocery business is a zero-sum game in America," said Sankaran.

The grocer cut its initial fiscal-year view in July and pulled its forecast altogether on Tuesday. It said it won't provide an updated outlook until it completes a comprehensive review of its business during its fourth quarter. The company reported second-quarter profit of $52 million, down from $169 million a year earlier.

Analysts expect that means Albertsons will soon return to the M&A market for the first time since its failed deal with Kroger. "We wouldn't be surprised if [Albertsons] attempts to sell banners/certain regions or real estate," said Kelly Bania of BMO Capital Markets.
Whitman is of a similar mind.

"We must also take a close look at our portfolio of banners, markets, assets and businesses, as well as potential strategic actions we can take to enhance shareholder value," she said. "Dramatic improvement is needed now."
